evidence_notes.note: This identifies the deceased as Aldric Marsh, a 47-year-old harbor merchant, anchoring the victim’s role in dockside commerce and bonded cargo. Knowing he is a merchant connected to harbor business makes the later paperwork about a midnight bonded delivery directly relevant to him and helps connect the crime to dock operations rather than a purely personal dispute. It also frames why someone involved in harbor administration and warehousing would have both access and reason to interact with him at odd hours. This clue does not name an attacker, but it establishes the victim’s identity and occupational context needed to interpret the ledger, warehouse activity, and witness sightings as part of the same event.

The post-mortem finding that Aldric died from a single deep chest wound consistent with a fixed-blade knife narrows the means to a stabbing instrument rather than poisoning or strangulation. It aligns tightly with later physical evidence recovered from the warehouse: an engraved knife whose blade profile matches the wound channel. By specifying a fixed-blade knife as the likely weapon type, this clue supports selecting means_blade and makes any suspect’s access to or ownership of such a knife central to the case. It also undercuts alternative theories involving rope or poison because the fatal injury is explicitly a blade wound, not ligature marks or toxic symptoms.

The estimated time of death between midnight and 2 a.m. is a key synchronization point tying together the documentary and eyewitness evidence. The shipping ledger records a “midnight delivery” to the riverside warehouse, and a witness reports seeing a limping man heading toward the warehouse gates around midnight. This window also conflicts with Silas Vane’s stated timeline of leaving at ten and going straight home, making his denial more suspicious. The time range helps establish opportunity: whoever was at or moving toward the warehouse around midnight is temporally placed near the likely time of the killing. It also supports the timeline claims that the encounter and stabbing occurred at midnight.

The ledger’s entry showing a midnight delivery of bonded cargo to the riverside warehouse, authorized and signed for by Silas Vane, places Silas in direct administrative control of an unusual, late-night warehouse transaction at exactly the time window of the murder. This provides a concrete “setup” mechanism: a pretext for being at the warehouse at midnight and for summoning someone like Aldric into a vulnerable location under the guise of cargo business. It also directly contradicts Silas’s interview claim that he knew nothing about a midnight delivery. While it does not itself prove violence, it strongly corroborates a clandestine activity connected to Silas, creating motive and opportunity consistent with the timeline claims.

By establishing that the handwriting throughout the ledger matches Silas Vane’s known signature on the front page, this clue strengthens the attribution of the midnight delivery authorization to Silas personally rather than to forgery or another harbor worker. It reinforces that the ledger entries—including the midnight bonded cargo delivery—are tied to Silas’s own recordkeeping and decisions. This reduces alternative explanations that the incriminating ledger entry was planted or misattributed, and it supports treating the ledger as reliable evidence of Silas’s involvement in late-night warehouse operations. In context with his denial of any midnight delivery, this clue supports an inference of deception and concealment about his movements and activities around the murder window.

The engraved knife recovered at the warehouse has a blade profile that exactly matches the wound channel described in the post-mortem—same width and serration pattern—providing direct physical linkage between the murder injury and a specific weapon. This is the strongest corroboration for means_blade and ties the killing to the warehouse location where the knife was found. It narrows the field from “a knife” to this knife, increasing evidentiary weight against whoever owned or controlled it. While matching profiles do not alone prove who held it at the moment of stabbing, in combination with the knife’s identifying engraving and the evidence placing Silas at midnight warehouse activity, it heavily implicates Silas as the user or disposer of the weapon.

The initials ‘S.V.’ engraved on the knife’s pommel associate the recovered weapon with Silas Vane by name initials, making it far more than a generic blade found near the scene. In context with the knife’s blade profile matching the fatal wound, the engraving suggests the murder weapon was Silas’s personal knife or at least marked as his. Found in the warehouse, it supports the idea that the killer was at the warehouse and had reason to conceal or stash the weapon there after the attack. This clue strengthens identity attribution: it is a tangible, personalized item pointing toward Silas rather than Finn, Mara, or Rex, none of whom are linked by initials or ownership marks in the evidence board.

The signed receipt showing Rex Bowman cleared a substantial debt to Aldric Marsh three months ago provides an important counterweight to a simple financial-motive theory against Rex. It documents that the debt was paid in full well before the murder, reducing the likelihood that an unpaid obligation drove Rex to kill Aldric. This does not prove Rex could not have other motives, but it undercuts the strongest obvious motive that might attach to him from dockside rumor. In the broader case, this clue helps shift suspicion away from Rex and toward evidence more directly tied to midnight warehouse activity and the personalized knife linked to Silas.

The bartender’s statement that Rex was agitated on the night of the murder and drank heavily until closing establishes demeanor and a possible alibi-adjacent detail, but it is not precise enough alone to place Rex at or away from the harbor between midnight and 2 a.m. It does show Rex was upset, which could raise suspicion; however, when weighed against the paid-in-full debt receipt, it becomes more consistent with general distress than a clear motive to kill Aldric. Crucially, this clue does not connect Rex to the warehouse, the ledger’s midnight delivery, or the murder weapon. Relative to the strong physical and documentary ties to Silas, this becomes weaker, circumstantial color rather than decisive inculpation.

Finn’s account that he found the body at first light near Pier 3 and that the blood had already gone dark supports the medical estimate that Aldric had been dead for hours. This observation is consistent with a death occurring around midnight to 2 a.m. and helps corroborate the timeline by independent witness perception rather than paperwork. It also frames the body’s location at the harbor, indicating the killing or disposal occurred near the piers, even if related to warehouse dealings. Finn’s role is that of a discoverer, not a participant; this clue provides timing corroboration and reduces the chance the death occurred shortly before dawn. It does not identify the assailant but supports the established window that aligns with Silas-linked midnight activity.

Finn’s statement that Aldric had a reputation for clean dealings and that he was not widely spoken of badly (aside from dock hands thinking he underpaid) helps contextualize motive. It suggests Aldric was not known as a swindler who routinely provoked violent retribution, weakening broad “victim deserved it” narratives. This makes the most plausible motive something specific and situational—such as exposure of wrongdoing—rather than long-standing personal vendettas. In combination with evidence of a clandestine midnight bonded cargo delivery tied to Silas, the clue supports the idea that Aldric’s conflict was likely related to harbor-side operations and illicit runs rather than his general reputation. It indirectly supports focusing on the person running “private cargo runs,” not on generalized dockside grievances.

Mara’s eyewitness report places a tall man with a pronounced limp crossing toward the warehouse gates around midnight, moving quickly as if to avoid being seen. This directly situates an individual heading to the warehouse at the critical time window established by the time-of-death estimate. The limp is a distinctive identifying feature that becomes crucial when later clarified as belonging to a specific person. The behavior described—hurrying and not wanting to be seen—also aligns with clandestine activity rather than routine work. On its own, this clue doesn’t name the suspect, but it provides a strong opportunity indicator and a physical description that can be matched to a particular character, supporting the case against the person known for that limp.

After being shown the ledger, Mara identifies it as the harbormaster’s office ledger “the one Silas keeps for his private cargo runs,” directly linking Silas to covert or unofficial shipping activity. She then explicitly matches the limp she saw around midnight to Silas Vane’s limp, stating she has known it for years and that it was him. This is a direct identification that connects the midnight warehouse-bound figure (from her earlier sighting) to Silas. It also strengthens the relevance of the ledger’s midnight delivery entry as part of Silas’s private operations rather than standard harbor business. This clue provides the clearest witness-based attribution placing Silas moving toward the warehouse at the relevant time.

Rex’s statement that he cleared his debt with Aldric three months ago and has nothing against him is a self-serving claim, but it is later supported by documentary evidence (the signed debt receipt). As such, it contributes to exonerating Rex from a straightforward debt-driven motive. While Rex could still be involved for other reasons, this claim aligns with the available paperwork and reduces the likelihood that he had a strong financial grievance compelling murder. In context with the stronger evidence pointing to Silas—ledger authorization, witness identification of Silas’s limp, and the knife marked ‘S.V.’—this clue helps narrow the suspect field by diminishing one of the more obvious alternative theories.

Rex reports that Silas has been acting strange for weeks and has been secretive about who goes in and out of the warehouse at night. This is not direct proof of murder, but it supplies pattern and context: unusual nocturnal warehouse traffic tied to Silas predates the killing. It supports the interpretation that the midnight delivery entry is part of an ongoing covert operation, and it makes the warehouse a focal point for clandestine activity controlled or overseen by Silas. As a third-party observation, it also helps corroborate Mara’s and the ledger’s implications without relying solely on official documents. This clue strengthens motive and opportunity by suggesting Silas had ongoing reasons to hide nighttime warehouse access and movements.

Silas’s claim that he was at the office doing accounts, left around ten, went straight home, and knows nothing about a midnight delivery functions as an alibi assertion and denial. The authoritative evidence board contains documentary evidence of a midnight delivery authorized and signed for by Silas and later confirmation that the ledger is associated with Silas’s private cargo runs, placing his denial in direct tension with recorded activity. The discrepancy suggests deception about his whereabouts or actions and implies consciousness of guilt or at least a desire to conceal midnight warehouse involvement. This clue is important not because it is reliable on its face, but because it can be impeached by the ledger and witness identification, strengthening the case that Silas lied about the critical timeframe.

The search warrant authorizing entry to any bonded warehouse in the dock district establishes that the warehouse search was lawful and that evidence recovered there—most notably the engraved knife—was obtained under official authority. While it does not directly identify the killer or weapon, it supports evidentiary integrity by showing investigators had proper authorization to access bonded warehouse spaces, reducing claims that the knife or other findings are inadmissible or improperly obtained. In the context of building a coherent case, this clue helps ensure that the physical weapon evidence from the warehouse can be relied upon in concluding means and suspect. It is procedural corroboration that underpins the legitimacy of the investigation’s key physical discovery.

Mara further identifies the limping figure as Silas and links the ledger to Silas’s private cargo runs, fitting the claim that Aldric threatened to expose an illegal run. The murder weapon is tied to Silas: a knife matching the wound, engraved “S.V.” Rex is weakened as a suspect by proof his debt was paid; Finn is only the finder; Mara is a witness.
